overview.title: 📖 Overview: Tracing Every Consequence
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 15a–15b
overview.hebrewSource: כְּמוֹ שֶׁתֹּאכַל אֶת הַצְּבִי וְאֶת הָאַיָּל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues yesterday's dispute over whether all consecrated animals require 'standing and valuation' before redemption, reconciling Rav's teaching with two competing traditions. It then derives, from the verse comparing disqualified consecrated animals to a gazelle and a hart, exactly which exemptions apply and which do not — including a surprising twist in how the prohibition on their fat is phrased. The Gemara confronts a genuinely difficult case, offspring conceived before but born after their mother's redemption, and closes by laying out two complete baraitot that track every consequence of blemish preceding or following consecration.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Rav taught: 'this is Rabbi Shimon's view' — but since everyone agrees a blemished-before-consecration animal can be redeemed after death, shouldn't he have said 'Rabbi Shimon's view and his disputants'?

lines.speaker: Resolution 1
lines.text: Rav follows Reish Lakish's version: the Rabbis hold Temple-maintenance items needed standing and valuation but altar items did not — so the mishna's burial rule can't be explained by the Rabbis at all, only by Rabbi Shimon.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But maybe 'must be buried' reflects a different rule — that one may not redeem sacrifices just to feed them to dogs — not 'standing and valuation' at all!

lines.speaker: Resolution 2
lines.text: Alternatively: Rav follows Rabbi Yoḥanan's version, where the Rabbis do require standing and valuation even for altar items — so the mishna fits the Rabbis fine, and Rav's phrasing stands as written.

slides.title: 🦌 Deriving Exemption From 'Gazelle and Hart'
slides.subtitle: Tracing exactly how far the comparison extends

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'As you eat the gazelle and the hart, so shall you eat' (Deuteronomy 12:22) teaches disqualified consecrated animals are exempt from firstborn status, like undomesticated game
2️⃣ Does it extend to priestly gifts too? Yes — naming both animals teaches both exemptions, since gifts (unlike firstborn) apply even to females
3️⃣ Does it extend to permitting their fat, like a gazelle's? No — the word 'ach' ('however') limits the comparison strictly to firstborn and gifts

4️⃣ Rava's twist: the Torah's odd phrase 'you shall not eat its blood' (not 'fat') actually teaches the fat prohibition — borrowing blood's language to show the fat carries the same karet penalty as blood, not merely lashes

slides.title: 🐣 Offspring Conceived Before, Born After Redemption
slides.subtitle: A genuinely difficult case — and a preemptive solution

nodes.content: ❓ A fetus conceived while its mother was still consecrated, but born AFTER her redemption — sacred, or not? And what can be done with it?
⚖️ If born BEFORE the mother's redemption: disputed whether it may be fully sacrificed, or only grazed until blemished and then redeemed

columns.label: Rav Huna
columns.content: If born AFTER redemption: gather it into a room and let it starve — it can't be sacrificed (deferred sanctity) and can't be redeemed (too weak a sanctity to transfer)

columns.label: Eretz Yisrael tradition
columns.content: Better: dedicate the still-unborn fetus to the SAME offering as its mother, just before she is redeemed — preempting the problem entirely

nodes.content: ✅ Reason for the preemptive dedication: a rabbinic decree, lest people raise entire flocks of forbidden, unusable offspring

slides.title: 📊 Two Full Baraitot, Side by Side
slides.subtitle: Every consequence, tracked in parallel

boxes.title: Blemish Preceded Consecration
items: Firstborn & gifts: obligated, before and after redemption
Shearing/labor: no lashes, even before redemption
Offspring fully non-sacred if born after redemption; redeemable unblemished if born before
May be dedicated to any sacrifice desired

boxes.title: Consecration Preceded Blemish
items: Firstborn & gifts: exempt, before and after redemption
Shearing/labor: full lashes, even before redemption
Offspring fully sacred; may not be redeemed while unblemished
May not be dedicated to any sacrifice but the same one as the mother

slides.title: 🎯 Can the Offspring Be Dedicated to Any Sacrifice?
slides.subtitle: Ravina's question to Rav Sheshet

nodes.content: ❓ Per the Eretz Yisrael practice of pre-dedicating a fetus before its mother's redemption — must it match the mother's offering, or can the owner choose freely?
📖 Rav Sheshet: it must match the mother's offering — derived by verbal analogy ('in your gates,' 'in your gates') to the law of a firstborn animal
✅ Just as a firstborn's identity is fixed by birth and cannot be reassigned to a chosen sacrifice, the same fixed identity applies here
📜 A baraita confirms Rav Sheshet's ruling as part of the complete comparison between the two categories of once-blemished consecrated animals

summary.principle: Every consequence of a consecrated animal's blemish — its obligations, its offspring's status, and whether it may be redeemed after death — flows from a single question: did the blemish come before or after consecration, and every downstream rule is derived with precision from that starting point.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Rav's teaching is reconciled with the mishna through two competing traditions about which consecrated animals require 'standing and valuation'
🦌 'Gazelle and hart' exempts disqualified consecrated animals from firstborn and gifts, but not from the fat prohibition

columns.content: 🐣 Offspring conceived before but born after redemption are best pre-empted by dedicating them before the mother is redeemed
🎯 Such offspring, once dedicated, are fixed to the mother's original offering, like a firstborn's fixed identity

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the order of blemish and consecration governs every rule — obligations, offspring, substitutes, and redemption after death

quiz.q: According to the version reconciling Rav with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, why can't the mishna's rule that unredeemed animals 'must be buried' be explained according to the Rabbis?
o: Because the Rabbis never discuss burial

Because, per that version, the Rabbis hold that altar-consecrated animals (unlike Temple-maintenance items) were not subject to 'standing and valuation,' so burial must reflect Rabbi Shimon's view alone
Because burial only applies to firstborn animals
Because the Rabbis always permit redemption after death
quiz.e: According to this version, since the Rabbis exempt altar-consecrated animals from 'standing and valuation,' the mishna's requirement of burial after death must be Rabbi Shimon's distinct position.

quiz.q: From which verse does the Gemara derive that disqualified consecrated animals are exempt from both firstborn status and priestly gifts?
o: 'You shall not muzzle an ox' (Deuteronomy 25:4)
'As you eat the gazelle and the hart, so shall you eat' (Deuteronomy 12:22), naming both animals to teach both exemptions
'Sanctify to Me all the firstborn' (Exodus 13:2)
There is no verse; it is derived by logic alone
quiz.e: The verse's mention of both a gazelle and a hart is read as teaching two separate exemptions — from firstborn status and from priestly gifts.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, what happens to the offspring of a disqualified consecrated animal conceived before but born after its mother's redemption?
o: It becomes fully non-sacred immediately
It is gathered into a room and left to starve, since it can neither be sacrificed nor redeemed
It is sacrificed on the altar regardless
It is given to a priest to raise
quiz.e: Rav Huna rules that such an offspring has deferred sanctity too weak to be sacrificed or redeemed, leaving starvation as the only outcome under his approach.

quiz.q: How does the Eretz Yisrael tradition (in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina) avoid Rav Huna's difficult outcome?
o: By selling the offspring to a gentile
By dedicating the still-unborn fetus to the same offering as its mother, just before her own redemption
By declaring all such offspring permanently non-sacred
By requiring the mother never be redeemed
quiz.e: Dedicating the fetus to the mother's own offering before her redemption preempts the problem, avoiding the impossible choice between sacrifice and redemption after birth.

quiz.q: According to Rav Sheshet, may the offspring of a consecration-preceded-blemish animal be dedicated to any sacrifice the owner chooses?
o: Yes, entirely at the owner's discretion
No — it must be dedicated to the same type of offering as its mother, derived by analogy to the fixed identity of a firstborn animal
No such offspring can ever be dedicated to anything
Only priests may decide its designation
quiz.e: Rav Sheshet derives via verbal analogy to firstborn law that the offspring's identity is fixed to match its mother's original offering, just as a firstborn cannot be reassigned to a different sacrifice.
